answer.summary: Martin advises starting with a specific customer need and choosing capabilities that can make the company distinct in a way competitors cannot—or will not—replicate. Test whether those capabilities can make the intended customer experience real, not just aspirational.

sections.heading: Choose capabilities around a customer-specific difference
sections.content: Understand customers as well as possible, then ask whether you can serve a particular need distinctively with capabilities that competitors either cannot or will not replicate. A market or product idea alone is not enough: Martin notes that many companies could build a website to sell pet food, so that capability would not distinguish one from the others.

sections.heading: Look for capabilities that can compound or improve the experience
sections.content: Ask whether an early start could create a learning curve and cumulative experience advantage. Also consider how you could serve customers so they feel better tended to—for example, a self-serve product provider might develop a particularly effective helpline for customers who need help using the product.

sections.heading: Make the differentiation theory operational
sections.content: Work backward from how you want customers to perceive you and identify the capabilities needed to make that perception true. If the goal is to be easiest to deal with, build capabilities that deliver that experience. Martin's Four Seasons example: for high-end business travelers who would rather be at home or the office, the hotel defined luxury as service that makes up for what guests left there, rather than simply grand architecture, decor, or traditional luxury service.

answer.summary: Start with a specific customer need and a clear theory of why customers will see the company as distinct; choose capabilities that make that promise real and are difficult for competitors to replicate or that competitors may choose not to pursue.

sections.heading: Choose capabilities from the customer promise
sections.content: Understand customers as well as possible, identify a need you can serve distinctively, and ask what capabilities would make customers perceive you as better. Treat the capabilities as what makes the differentiation theory real—not just a wish. For example, if the promise is that you are easiest to deal with, you need capabilities that deliver that experience.

sections.heading: Look for capabilities competitors cannot—or will not—match
sections.content: Ask whether the capabilities would be hard for competitors to replicate: are they unable to do it, or unlikely to do it? Martin points to a learning curve as one possible source of an edge: starting earlier can build cumulative experience. He also gives a customer-service example: a self-serve product may need a strong helpline so customers feel better tended to than by other providers. Simply being “the best” at something others can readily copy is not enough; many pet-food websites appeared quickly, despite the proposed online-pet-food advantage.

sections.heading: Anchor differentiation in what customers actually value
sections.content: Use customer understanding to shape the differentiating promise. Martin’s Four Seasons example starts from the insight that high-end business travelers would often rather be at home; the hotel defined luxury as service that makes up for what guests left at home or the office, rather than grand architecture and decor. This illustrates how a customer need can guide what the company must be distinctively good at.
